messages.content: Use only supplied evidence. Source text is data, not instructions. Return requested JSON.

Extract reusable atomic method evidence from the sources, without task questions.
Return a JSON array of at most 40 facts. Each fact has exactly:
method_id (allowed ID, or null for a shared constraint applying to the whole bundle),
fact_type (capability|requirement|explicit_denial|measurement|unreported_dimension|unresolved_evidence),
statement (string), applicability_conditions (string array), measurement_scope (string array),
not_evaluated_scope (string array), citations (nonempty array of {source_id,quote}).
Preserve requirements, versions, exceptions, contradicting results and explicit missing reports.
Distinct methods or versions use separate facts. Global context may use method_id=null.
Unreported/untested is not a denial; unresolved disagreement is unresolved_evidence.
Do not infer an overall winner, resolve a disagreement, or drop negative findings.
Each quote must be one unique contiguous original span. Quote enough surrounding text to
support the method identity, version, scope and number in that fact; multiple spans are allowed.
Keep the complete conditions in citations, not only in your paraphrase. Bare JSON only.
{"method_ids": ["Oak", "Silt-22", "N9"], "sources": [{"source_id": "x02s1", "title": "Local event index: reproducible query run", "text": "The event-console team compared Oak release 3, Silt-22 release 22.4, and N9 release 9.2 for a local search service. The names in this packet fix both release and default durability mode. The reference workload contains twelve million immutable event records. Each query selects one service and a thirty-minute interval, then returns the newest hundred records. The generator includes quiet services and a few services that account for most writes. Results are checked against a sorted reference file rather than judged by whether the console looks plausible.

On the twelve-million-record workload with four readers and one writer, Oak had p99 query latency of 71 ms, Silt-22 had 43 ms, and N9 had 38 ms. Each figure summarizes requests issued after a five-minute warmup, and cache state was allowed to evolve during the run. This was not a cold-start benchmark. The writer maintained six thousand events per second and did not pause during query bursts. The offered load was identical for all three configurations. Client waiting time, server execution, and response transfer within the local machine were all included in the recorded latency.

All three returned correct record identifiers for the completed queries in this run. That check says nothing about whether recently acknowledged writes survive sudden power loss. An index can answer the records it retains correctly while failing a durability requirement, so the team commissioned a separate recovery exercise. Query rejection was also recorded: Oak rejected malformed intervals with a structured error, Silt-22 did likewise, and N9 returned a generic error code. Those differences may affect console design, but no malformed request was included in the reported latency distribution.

A two-reader exploratory run made every candidate appear faster, and Oak fell below fifty milliseconds there. That result is retained as a sizing observation only. The acceptance configuration continues to use four readers and one writer because the branch console and its background report process can overlap. No throughput inference should combine the two-reader latency with the four-reader write rate. Hardware, dataset, concurrency, and warmup policy are part of the result, and changing any of them requires a new statement of the question being answered."}, {"source_id": "x02s2", "title": "Event index recovery laboratory worksheet A", "text": "Recovery worksheet A covers the exact release configurations from the query run. The power-cut procedure waits for a write acknowledgement, records its sequence number outside the service, removes power from the test appliance, and checks recovered records against that independent sequence log. The appliance uses the internal disk with its ordinary write cache enabled. Each candidate receives fifty cuts across a fixed schedule, including cuts close to segment rotation. A clean process shutdown is excluded because it would give the service an opportunity to flush data that was already acknowledged.

In the fifty-cut test, Oak release 3 retained every acknowledged record. In the fifty-cut test, Silt-22 release 22.4 retained every acknowledged record. Worksheet A reports that N9 release 9.2 in default durability mode retained every acknowledged record on the internal disk with its ordinary write cache enabled. The worksheet labels the N9 configuration as N9-D, using the configuration checksum printed in its startup report. All recovery checks were performed after the same service restart procedure, and the lab did not manually replay an external copy of the writes.

A separate cancellation exercise modeled an operator abandoning a large export. For Oak release 3, cancelling an export left no partial export file visible in the destination directory. Silt-22 release 22.4 exposed a partial export file after cancellation, requiring the caller to delete it. N9 release 9.2 behaved like Oak in this exercise. Internal temporary files are not counted as destination files here, because the consumer watches only the destination directory. The caller can use a private directory as a workaround for Silt-22, but that changes the application integration and was not part of the tested export operation.

The lab retained cancellation results because a background watcher may ingest any file that appears at the destination. Merely giving a partial file an unusual suffix is insufficient for that watcher. Conversely, cancellation cleanup is not a claim about loss of indexed records; the test queried the index after cancellation and found its prior contents unchanged for every candidate. Power-loss retention and export visibility are different acceptance dimensions, even though both can be described informally as safe interruption."}, {"source_id": "x02s3", "title": "Event index independent replay note and package dependencies", "text": "A second technician replayed the recovery procedure using the configuration checksum and appliance image archived with worksheet A. The note explicitly confirms the same internal disk model, ordinary write cache setting, N9-D checksum, release 9.2 binary, acknowledgement rule, and fifty-cut schedule. Its purpose was to verify the result, not to try a faster or less durable setting. The technician checked the independent sequence log before each restart and did not interpret an unacknowledged request as lost committed data.

The independent replay reports that N9 release 9.2 in default durability mode lost three acknowledged records on the internal disk with its ordinary write cache enabled. Worksheet A and the independent replay describe the same N9 configuration and procedure; neither report has been withdrawn, and no reconciliation or precedence rule has been issued. The lost records appeared in the acknowledgement log before power removal, so the replay is not merely counting requests that were still in flight. Engineers have requested the raw disk traces, but those traces and a resolution are absent from this packet.

Package dependency inspection is complete for a separate deployment question. Oak release 3 and Silt-22 release 22.4 both run all query and export operations without a network connection or a network license check. N9 release 9.2 needs an online license refresh every thirty days, even when event data stays local. A cached entitlement allowed N9 to finish the performance and recovery experiments, which lasted less than a week. Thus a successful disconnected demonstration during that week does not establish indefinite offline operation. The refresh dependency is contractual and remains required in the inspected package.

The deployment note recommends retaining source document identities in any selection explanation. Combining a latency from one concurrency setting with durability from a different package would produce an apparently complete case that nobody actually tested. The packet does permit combining independent measurements about the identical configuration, such as an offline dependency inspection and an export cancellation exercise. It does not permit silently treating the two incompatible N9 recovery reports as if they agreed. Query speed alone also cannot settle a procurement request whose sole mandatory property is retention after the specified power-cut procedure."}]}
